questions.stem: Which three strategies make vaccine pathogens harmless?

options.text: Killing the pathogen, weakening it, or using fragments of it
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Antibiotics are treatment, not vaccine design.
Freezing is storage, not harmlessness.
Dyes do not disarm anything.
Attenuation describes the pathogen, not the route.

options.text: One using a weakened version of the pathogen
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Killed and weakened are separate strategies.
Fragment vaccines are a third strategy.

questions.stem: By which routes can a vaccine be administered?

options.explanation: Raw pathogen is neither harmless nor a vaccine.
Contact does not administer vaccines.
Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Two other routes exist.

questions.stem: Why can a killed pathogen still train the immune system?

options.text: Because dead cells keep dividing slowly
options.explanation: Dead means no division.

options.text: Because antibodies are already in the dose
options.explanation: The body makes the antibodies.
Vaccines carry antigens, not antibodies.

options.text: Its antigens remain on the surface, triggering the same recognition
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

questions.stem: What public-health effect have vaccines achieved?

options.text: Drastic reductions in some diseases and eradication of others worldwide
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Vaccines prevent; they are not cures.
The reductions are dramatic and documented.
Immunity from vaccination applies across ages.

questions.stem: Define a vaccine in one sentence.
questions.modelAnswer: A vaccine contains a harmless version of a pathogen that builds immunity to the infectious disease it causes.

questions.stem: State the word for a weakened-pathogen vaccine.
questions.modelAnswer: An attenuated vaccine uses a weakened version of the pathogen.

questions.stem: Explain why fragment vaccines can work despite carrying no whole pathogen.
questions.modelAnswer: Because the antigen markers alone are enough for lymphocytes to recognise and respond, so immunity forms without any living agent present.

questions.stem: A new vaccine uses only surface protein fragments. Which strategy is this, and why is it safe?
questions.modelAnswer: It is the fragments strategy, safe because no whole pathogen — living or dead — is present to replicate or cause disease.

questions.stem: Which cells recognise the antigens in a vaccine?

options.explanation: Red cells carry oxygen.
Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Phagocytes engulf non-specifically; recognition with specificity is lymphocyte work.
Platelets clot; they do not recognise antigens.

questions.stem: What do activated lymphocytes produce against the vaccine antigens?

options.explanation: The lymphocytes respond to antigens; they do not make them.
Enzyme release belongs to phagocytes.
Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Specificity is the defining feature.

questions.stem: What forms from the lymphocytes during vaccination?

options.explanation: The vaccine's harmless form does not multiply.
Platelets are unrelated to memory.
No new organs form.

options.text: Memory cells that persist in the blood for many years
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

questions.stem: How does the secondary response compare with the first?

options.text: Sooner, faster and in greater quantity of antibodies
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
It is faster on every count.
Memory makes it different.

options.text: Weaker, since the antigen is familiar
options.explanation: Familiarity strengthens, not weakens.

questions.stem: Why does a vaccinated person stay healthy when the real pathogen arrives?

options.text: Because antibodies from the vaccine dose remain forever
options.explanation: The dose's antibodies fade; memory cells persist.

options.text: The rapid memory-cell response destroys the pathogen before it can cause disease
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: Because the pathogen cannot enter the body at all
options.explanation: Entry happens; the response wins the race.

options.text: Because the vaccine blocks the airways
options.explanation: No physical blocking occurs.

questions.stem: State what memory cells do upon a later infection.
questions.modelAnswer: They enable antibody production against the pathogen to begin sooner, run faster and reach a greater quantity.

questions.stem: Name the long-lasting lymphocyte type produced by vaccination.
questions.modelAnswer: Memory cells are the long-lasting lymphocytes left after vaccination.

questions.stem: Explain why circulating memory cells matter more than the vaccine dose's own antibodies.
questions.modelAnswer: Because the dose's antibodies decline within weeks, while memory cells persist for years and can launch fresh antibody production whenever the antigen reappears.

questions.stem: Sketch the antibody graph after vaccination and later infection. Describe its two peaks.
questions.modelAnswer: A small first peak follows vaccination as antibodies form slowly; the second peak after infection rises higher and sooner because memory cells drive a faster, larger response.
